reason: The sources support a compelling 45-second story with over 15 cross-verified claims across multiple independent websites.
story: In 1906, wealthy businessman Percival Lowell initiated a search at his observatory in Flagstaff, Arizona, for an unseen Planet X. Though Lowell died in 1916 without finding it, the search resumed years later when director V. M. Slipher hired Clyde Tombaugh, a young man from Kansas. Using a new 13-inch photographic telescope funded by Abbott Lawrence Lowell, Tombaugh discovered Pluto in February 1930. Pluto was hailed as the ninth planet, but doubts grew over time as scientists discovered its small size and tenuous atmosphere of nitrogen, methane, and carbon monoxide. In 2005, astronomers discovered Eris, a body more massive than Pluto in the Kuiper belt. This prompted the International Astronomical Union in 2006 to redefine a planet as a round body that has cleared its orbital neighborhood. Because Pluto failed this criterion, it was reclassified as a dwarf planet. NASA's New Horizons spacecraft flew by Pluto in July 2015, revealing a complex world featuring the giant nitrogen-ice basin Sputnik Planitia.
angle: In 2006, the International Astronomical Union demoted Pluto to a dwarf planet because it failed to clear its orbital neighborhood, yet NASA's New Horizons flyby revealed an active world harboring a 1,000-kilometer basin of solid nitrogen ice.

claims.claim: Percival Lowell founded the Lowell Observatory in Flagstaff, Arizona, and began searching for an undiscovered planet called Planet X.
Percival Lowell died in 1916 before his search for Planet X could be completed.
Lowell Observatory director V. M. Slipher hired Clyde Tombaugh, a young man from Kansas, to take over the search for Planet X.
Abbott Lawrence Lowell provided funding to build a new 13-inch photographic telescope for the observatory's planet search.
Clyde Tombaugh discovered Pluto in February 1930 at the Lowell Observatory.
Pluto is located in the Kuiper belt, a region of icy bodies orbiting beyond Neptune.
Pluto follows an eccentric orbit that periodically brings it closer to the Sun than Neptune.
Pluto possesses a tenuous atmosphere composed primarily of nitrogen, with small amounts of methane and carbon monoxide.
In 2005, astronomers announced the discovery of Eris, a distant object more massive than Pluto.
In 2006, the International Astronomical Union adopted a formal definition of a planet requiring a body to be round and to have cleared its orbital neighborhood.
Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet because its mass is insufficient to clear the neighborhood around its orbit.
NASA launched the New Horizons mission in 2006 to explore Pluto and the outer solar system.
New Horizons performed its close flyby of Pluto in July 2015 under principal investigator Alan Stern.
New Horizons discovered that Pluto contains a massive nitrogen-ice impact basin named Sputnik Planitia.
New Horizons finished transmitting all of its Pluto flyby data back to Earth in October 2016.
Charon is the largest moon orbiting Pluto.

disputed: Clyde Tombaugh's exact age upon arriving at Lowell Observatory differs across sources (S1 states 23, S2 states 22); scripts should refer to him generally as a young man from Kansas.
The exact discovery year of Eris varies slightly between sources (S1 and S2 cite 2005, S5 cites 2003); scripts should reference its announcement in the mid-2000s.

The premise that Pluto has not completed a single orbit since discovery and won't until 2178 is only stated in Wikipedia sources (S1, S2); because it lacks a second independent domain source, it must be omitted from official script claims.
